openingProblem.problem: In 1941 the German army captured millions of Soviet soldiers and reached the outskirts of Moscow and Leningrad. Four years later the Red Army stood in Berlin. How did Stalin's state survive and win, and what did victory cost its people?

chunks.title: Catastrophe and survival, 1941–1942
chunks.body:
In June 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union. The first months were a catastrophe. The Germans captured some 5.5 million Soviet soldiers during the war, three-quarters of them in the first seven months; at Kiev in September 1941 alone they took 750,000 prisoners, of whom only 22,000 survived. In 1956 Khrushchev would accuse Stalin of leaving the country unprepared for the invasion.

The state fought back by moving the economy east. Between 17 and 25 million people, and 1,523 large defence factories, were evacuated to the Urals, Western Siberia and Central Asia. Because Stalin had feared that planning for evacuation would encourage defeatism, it was improvised and chaotic, and many evacuees died of hunger and disease. Yet the relocation of industry made possible the defence production on which victory depended; the Russian historian G. A. Kumanev concludes that its main goal "was achieved".

**Leningrad** was besieged from September 1941 for two and a half years. Supplies came only across the frozen Lake Ladoga, the "road of life". In March 1942 the city buried 89,968 people and in April 102,497. Stalin rallied the population not only with communist slogans but with the language of Russian nationalism and history.

This mattered because the regime survived the first catastrophic year by mobilising people and industry on an enormous scale, which meant that the war became a test the Soviet system passed at a terrible human cost.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The invasion caught the USSR unprepared.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Red Army did not collapse.

chunks.title: Turning the tide: Stalingrad and Kursk, 1942–1943
chunks.body:
In summer 1942 Germany struck south towards the Caucasus oil fields, and the German Sixth Army attacked **Stalingrad** on the Volga. After two months of bombardment it held nine-tenths of the ruined city, but the defenders, bound by Stalin's **Order No. 227** ("Not One Step Back!"), fought house by house. On 19 November about a million Soviet troops under **Zhukov** attacked both German flanks and trapped some 250,000 enemy soldiers. On **2 February 1943** Paulus surrendered with 110,000 survivors. Soviet casualties were about 750,000. After Stalingrad, the war's outcome was no longer in doubt.

In July 1943 the Germans tried once more at **Kursk**, in the largest tank battle of the war. The Red Army, with 1.3 million men and 3,600 tanks, held the attacks and went over to the offensive; the Germans lost 30 of their 50 divisions. Kiev was liberated on 6 November 1943. The historian James von Geldern argues that Kursk, rather than the Normandy landings that western historians usually stress, was the more likely turning point of the war.

The Soviet Union did not fight alone. From October 1941 the United States sent Lend-Lease aid, and by the end of 1943 the Big Three met at **Tehran**, where they agreed the outlines of post-war Europe. But Stalin repeatedly complained that the western allies delayed the "second front" in France until 1944.

This mattered because the Red Army broke the German offensive on its own soil in 1942–43, which meant that the Soviet Union emerged from the war as a victor with a decisive claim on the shape of post-war Europe.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Allied aid helped the Soviet war effort.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The second front came only in 1944.

chunks.title: The regime at war: nationalism and deportation
chunks.body:
The war changed the regime's language but not its methods. Stalin rallied the population with traditional Russian patriotism: heroes of the Russian past such as Ivan the Terrible were celebrated, and Eisenstein's film of Ivan's life won a Stalin Prize in 1944. In May 1943 the Comintern, the organisation of world communist parties, was dissolved, a gesture welcomed by Stalin's western allies.

At the same time the NKVD pursued whole peoples. In 1941 at least 400,000 Volga Germans were deported east. In 1943–44 about **one million** Chechens, Ingush, Karachai, Balkars, Kalmyks, Meskhetian Turks and Crimean Tatars were deported to Kazakhstan and Central Asia, collectively accused of collaborating with the Germans. In February 1944 almost the entire Chechen and Ingush populations were deported in a single night; many died on the way. Only in 1957 were most allowed to return, and the Crimean Tatars and Meskhetian Turks were not.

Soviet prisoners of war were also treated as suspects. Of 5.5 million Soviet citizens repatriated by 1953, one in five was shot or sent to the Gulag.

This mattered because the regime combined patriotic mobilisation with collective punishment, which meant that victory strengthened the state's claim to legitimacy without ending its habits of repression.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Patriotism replaced revolutionary internationalism in wartime propaganda.
Returning prisoners were treated as suspects.

chunks.title: Victory and hardship: the post-war years, 1945–1953
chunks.body:
Victory came at a staggering price. The Soviet Union lost **8.6 million** men and women under arms and, in total, about **27 million** people, around one in eleven of its pre-war population.

Peace brought new hardship. By 1945 collective farms had only 42 per cent of their pre-war horses and 38 per cent of their working-age men. In 1946 a drought cut the grain harvest to 39.6 million tons, against 95.5 million in 1940; yet procurement quotas stayed high and private plots were taken back, and famine struck in 1946–47. When rationing was abolished on 14 December 1947, a currency reform wiped out many people's savings, and the change, Lewis Siegelbaum writes, "belied hopes for improvements in living conditions". Of eleven million soldiers, 8.5 million were demobilised over three years, many into unemployment and homelessness.

Politically, the regime tightened its grip. Andrei Zhdanov's campaign of 1946–48 attacked writers and "cosmopolitanism"; a 1947 law banned marriage to foreigners; Lysenko's triumph in 1948 halted genetics; and after Zhdanov's death a purge struck the Leningrad party. When Stalin died on **5 March 1953**, the "Doctors' Plot" seemed to herald a new purge; his successors formed a "collective leadership".

This mattered because victory brought the Soviet Union great-power status but little relief for its people, which meant that Stalin's successors inherited a strong state and an exhausted, impoverished society.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The war's human cost was enormous.

useItInAnEssay.prove: In 1946 drought cut the harvest to 39.6 million tons against 95.5 million in 1940, yet procurement quotas stayed high, and famine followed in 1946–47.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the regime continued to put the state's needs before the population's, so peace did not bring the improvement many expected.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, rationing was abolished in December 1947, which the regime presented as a sign of recovery.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The post-war years therefore showed a victorious state ruling an exhausted society.

modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did peace bring relief? Little: hardship continued under different causes.

segments.text: Peace brought the Soviet people little economic relief after the hardships of war.
During the war Leningrad buried over 100,000 people a month in spring 1942, whereas after it the 1946 drought and high quotas caused famine in 1946–47.
This meant that hunger continued in peacetime, so the end of rationing in December 1947 belied hopes for better living conditions.
However, the causes differed: wartime hardship came from invasion and siege, post-war hardship from drought, labour shortages and state policy.
The two periods were therefore alike in hardship but different in cause, with the state's priorities making peace almost as hard as war.

essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons for Soviet victory in the Great Patriotic War between 1941 and 1945.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which reason mattered most, and how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The Soviet Union won because it saved and expanded its war industry through evacuation, mobilised its population through patriotism and coercion, defeated the Germans in decisive battles at Stalingrad and Kursk, and received allied aid.
modelPlan.counter: Victory came at the cost of about 27 million lives.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which mattered most? War industry, without which the battles could not have been won.

segments.text: Soviet victory rested above all on the survival and growth of its war industry.
In 1941–42 between 17 and 25 million people and 1,523 large defence plants were moved east, and Kumanev concludes the evacuation achieved its goal.
This meant that the Red Army could be re-equipped beyond German reach, so it could fight and win at Stalingrad and Kursk.
However, victory also required patriotic and coercive mobilisation, Lend-Lease aid from October 1941, and enormous sacrifice, with about 27 million dead.
War industry was therefore the foundation, with mobilisation and the decisive battles building on it.
